hand: Receptors in the skin of the little finger and in the muscles pick up fine touch, vibration and joint position.
The 1st-order axon runs in the ulnar nerve, the inferior trunk and the C8 root to its cell body.
The 1st-order cell body (pseudounipolar) sits in the dorsal root ganglion, outside the cord.
The axon enters by the dorsal root and climbs the same-side fasciculus cuneatus (arm fibres, lateral) without a synapse.
It ends in the same-side cuneate nucleus of the caudal medulla: the first synapse.
The 2nd-order cell body sits in the cuneate nucleus, on the same side as the stimulus.
The 2nd-order axons sweep ventromedially and cross the midline in the caudal medulla: the sensory decussation.
The crossed fibres climb the contralateral medial lemniscus through the medulla, pons and midbrain to the thalamus.
The 3rd-order cell body sits in the ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus, opposite the stimulus.
Thalamocortical axons leave the VPL laterally toward the internal capsule.
They pass through the internal capsule‹ (posterior limb)›.
They fan out through the corona radiata to the postcentral gyrus, hand area on the lateral surface.
The signal arrives in S1 (BA 3, 1, 2) of the hemisphere opposite the stimulus.

hand: Free nerve endings in the skin of the little finger respond to pain, temperature and itch.
Aδ (sharp pain) and C (dull, burning pain) fibres run in the ulnar nerve, the inferior trunk and the C8 root to their cell bodies.
The 1st-order cell body sits in the dorsal root ganglion, outside the cord.
The axon enters by the dorsal root‹ and Lissauer's tract› and synapses in the same-side dorsal horn: the marginal zone (Aδ) or the substantia gelatinosa onto nucleus proprius cells (C).
The 2nd-order cell body sits in the dorsal horn (marginal zone or nucleus proprius) on the same side as the stimulus.
The 2nd-order axon crosses the midline in the anterior (ventral) white commissure, near the level of entry.
It climbs the contralateral anterolateral (spinothalamic) tract in the anterior and lateral funiculi, then the lateral brainstem tegmentum, to the thalamus.
The 3rd-order cell body sits in the ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus, opposite the stimulus.
Thalamocortical axons leave the VPL laterally toward the internal capsule.
They pass through the internal capsule‹ (posterior limb)›.
They fan out through the corona radiata to the postcentral gyrus, hand area on the lateral surface.
The signal arrives in S1 (BA 3, 1, 2) of the hemisphere opposite the stimulus.

Muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs in the foot muscles signal muscle length and contraction (unconscious proprioception).
The 1st-order Aα (Ia/Ib) axon runs in the medial plantar, tibial and sciatic nerves to the L5 ganglion.
The 1st-order cell body sits in the dorsal root ganglion, outside the cord.
The axon enters by the dorsal root, climbs the dorsal column to the lumbar cord and synapses in the same-side column of Clarke (C8-L2).
The 2nd-order cell body sits in the ipsilateral column of Clarke at the base of the dorsal horn.
Its axon climbs the same-side dorsal spinocerebellar tract in the lateral funiculus, without crossing.
At the medulla the tract enters the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
The fibres end in the cerebellar cortex of the same side.
Afferent pathways to the cerebellum stay on the same side, unlike most sensory pathways to the cortex.

*: Receptors in the skin of the face detect fine touch and vibration; here the cheek, served by the maxillary division (V2).
The 1st-order axon runs back in the maxillary nerve, one of the three divisions (V1, V2, V3).
The 1st-order cell body sits in the trigeminal ganglion (middle cranial fossa), not in a dorsal root ganglion.
The central process enters the lateral pons in the sensory root of the trigeminal nerve.
The axon synapses in the principal sensory nucleus of V in the rostral pons, on the same side.
The 2nd-order cell body sits in the ipsilateral principal sensory nucleus.
The 2nd-order axons cross the midline in the pons.
They ascend as the trigeminal lemniscus, part of the medial lemniscus, to the contralateral VPM.
The 3rd-order cell body sits in the contralateral VPM nucleus, the face's relay (the body's is the VPL).
The thalamocortical axon leaves the VPM laterally.
It runs up the internal capsule.
It fans out in the corona radiata to the face area of the postcentral gyrus (BA 3,1,2).
The face area lies low on the postcentral gyrus, opposite the stimulated side.
Receptors in the skin of the face detect pain and temperature; here the cheek, served by the maxillary division (V2).
The 1st-order axon runs back in the maxillary nerve, one of the three divisions (V1, V2, V3).
The 1st-order cell body sits in the trigeminal ganglion (middle cranial fossa), not in a dorsal root ganglion.
The central process enters the lateral pons in the sensory root of the trigeminal nerve.
The axon descends on the same side in the spinal trigeminal tract (lateral tegmentum) and synapses in the spinal nucleus, largest in the caudal medulla.
The 2nd-order cell body sits in the ipsilateral spinal trigeminal nucleus, a long column through pons and medulla.
The 2nd-order axons cross the midline just after the nucleus.
They ascend in the trigeminothalamic tract, beside the anterolateral (spinothalamic) tract, to the contralateral VPM.
The 3rd-order cell body sits in the contralateral VPM nucleus, the face's relay (the body's is the VPL).
The thalamocortical axon leaves the VPM laterally.
It runs up the internal capsule.
It fans out in the corona radiata to the face area of the postcentral gyrus (BA 3,1,2).
The face area lies low on the postcentral gyrus, opposite the stimulated side.
Touching the cornea stimulates sensory endings of the ophthalmic division (V1).
The 1st-order axon runs back from the cornea in V1 through the orbit.
Its cell body sits in the trigeminal ganglion.
The axon enters the pons and descends to the spinal trigeminal nucleus, whose neurons project to the facial nucleus of both sides, one set crossing the midline.
Both facial nuclei drive CN VII to the eyelids: one eye senses the touch, both eyelids close.
Each facial nucleus sends its axons in CN VII to the orbicularis oculi.
Both orbicularis oculi muscles contract: both eyelids close.
A tap on the chin stretches the masseter and fires its muscle spindles.
The 1st-order axon runs back in the mandibular nerve (V3) and passes through the trigeminal ganglion without a cell body there.
Its cell body is inside the CNS, in the mesencephalic nucleus of V: the only primary sensory neurons inside the brain.
Its central branch synapses directly on the motor nucleus of V: a monosynaptic reflex.
The lower motor neuron's cell body sits in the motor nucleus of V in the pons.
Its axon leaves in the motor root and V3 to the masseter.
The masseter contracts and the jaw closes; the loop stops us biting down too hard.
